claim: Kinesin-3 is a family of microtubule-dependent motor proteins that transport various cargos within the cell.
source: Kinesin-3 is a family of microtubule-dependent motor proteins that transport various cargos within the cell.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinesin-3 function that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Both KLP-6 and UNC-104 are predominantly monomeric in solution.
source: Both KLP-6 and UNC-104 are predominantly monomeric in solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass photometry data shown in the manuscript (Figures 1C, 4C, 5C).

claim: Non-processive KLP-6 monomer is converted to a processive motor when artificially dimerized.
source: As previously shown for UNC-104, non-processive KLP-6 monomer is converted to a processive motor when artificially dimerized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing KLP-6(1-390)LZ exhibits processive movement (Figure 3).

claim: Releasing the autoinhibition is sufficient to trigger dimerization of monomeric UNC-104 at nanomolar concentrations.
source: We present evidence that releasing the autoinhibition is sufficient to trigger dimerization of monomeric UNC-104 at nanomolar concentrations, which results in processive movement of UNC-104 on microtubules, although it has long been thought that enrichment in the phospholipid microdomain on cargo vesicles is required for the dimerization and processive movement of UNC-104.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry and single molecule motility assays of UNC-104(1-653)(E412K) (Figure 5).

claim: KLP-6 remains a non-processive monomer even when its autoinhibition is unlocked.
source: In contrast, KLP-6 remains to be a non-processive monomer even when its autoinhibition is unlocked, suggesting a requirement of other factors for full activation.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry and TIRF assays showing KLP-6(1-587)(D458A) is monomeric and non-processive (Figure 4).

claim: A coiled-coil domain called CC2 is required for the efficient dimerization and processive movement of UNC-104.
source: By examining the differences between KLP-6 and UNC-104, we identified a coiled-coil domain called coiled-coil 2 (CC2) that is required for the efficient dimerization and processive movement of UNC-104.
evidence: This is supported by data showing UNC-104(1-594) lacking CC2 does not dimerize efficiently and has reduced processivity compared to UNC-104(1-653) (Figure 7).

claim: The kinesin-3 family is mainly involved in intracellular transport, including axonal transport of synaptic materials, lysosomal transport, mitochondrial transport, and intraflagellar transport of mechanoreceptor complexes.
source: Among kinesins, the kinesin-3 family is mainly involved in intracellular transport, including axonal transport of synaptic materials, lysosomal transport, mitochondrial transport, and intraflagellar transport of mechanoreceptor complexes (Chiba et al., 2023; Guardia et al., 2016; Morsci and Barr, 2011; Nangaku et al., 1994; Okada et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: C. elegans has three members of the kinesin-3 family: UNC-104, KLP-4, and KLP-6.
source: C. elegans has three members of the kinesin-3 family: UNC-104, KLP-4, and KLP-6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans kinesin-3 family members.

claim: UNC-104 transports synaptic vesicle precursors, mature synaptic vesicles, and pre-synaptic membrane proteins in the axon.
source: UNC-104 transports synaptic vesicle precursors, mature synaptic vesicles, and pre-synaptic membrane proteins in the axon (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991; Oliver et al., 2022; Otsuka et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian orthologs of UNC-104, KIF1A and KIF1Bβ, play a role in the axonal transport of synaptic materials.
source: Its mammalian orthologs, KIF1A and KIF1Bβ, also play a role in the axonal transport of synaptic materials (Niwa et al., 2008; Okada et al., 1995; Zhao et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in KIF1A and KIF1Bβ have been associated with congenital disorders.
source: Because mutations in KIF1A and KIF1Bβ have been associated with congenital disorders (Boyle et al., 2021; Budaitis et al., 2021; Klebe et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2001), C. elegans has been used to study the molecular mechanisms of pathogenesis (Anazawa et al., 2022; Chiba et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: KLP-4 is responsible for the transport of glutamate receptor GLR-1 in the dendrite.
source: KLP-4, on the other hand, is responsible for the transport of glutamate receptor called GLR-1 in the dendrite.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KLP-4 function.

claim: The transport of GLR-1 is significantly reduced in klp-4 mutant worms.
source: The transport of GLR-1 is significantly reduced in klp-4 mutant worms (Monteiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KLP-6 is an invertebrate specific kinesin-3.
source: KLP-6 is an invertebrate specific kinesin-3 and transports a mechanosensory receptor complex in male cilia (Morsci and Barr, 2011; Peden and Barr, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KLP-6 supported by citations.

claim: KLP-6 transports a mechanosensory receptor complex in male cilia.
source: KLP-6 is an invertebrate specific kinesin-3 and transports a mechanosensory receptor complex in male cilia (Morsci and Barr, 2011; Peden and Barr, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanoreceptor complex transported by KLP-6 consists of LOV-1 and PKD-2, orthologs of mammalian polycystin-1 and polycystin-2.
source: This mechanoreceptor complex consists of LOV-1 and PKD-2, orthologs of mammalian polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 (Barr et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in PKD-1 or PKD-2 gene cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in humans.
source: In human, mutations in PKD-1 or PKD-2 gene which encodes polycystin-1 or polycystin-2 cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (Hughes et al., 1995; Mochizuki et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in klp-6 gene lead to the reduction of LOV-1 and PKD-2 from the cilia and male infertility.
source: In worms, mutations in klp-6 gene lead to the reduction of LOV-1 and PKD-2 from the cilia and the male infertility because the mechanoreceptor complex is essential for male worms to locate the hermaphrodite vulva during mating behavior (Peden and Barr, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 and KLP-6 are regulated by a monomer-to-dimer conversion mechanism.
source: It has been proposed that these motors are regulated by a monomer-to-dimer conversion mechanism (Al-Bassam et al., 2003; Tomishige et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 dimers, which are stabilized by fusing with a coiled-coil domain of kinesin-1, exhibit plus-end directed movement on microtubules.
source: UNC-104 dimers, which are stabilized by fusing with a coiled-coil domain of kinesin-1, exhibit plus-end directed movement on microtubules, whereas purified UNC-104 monomers show only one-dimensional diffusion (Soppina et al., 2014; Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Purified UNC-104 monomers show only one-dimensional diffusion.
source: UNC-104 dimers, which are stabilized by fusing with a coiled-coil domain of kinesin-1, exhibit plus-end directed movement on microtubules, whereas purified UNC-104 monomers show only one-dimensional diffusion (Soppina et al., 2014; Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 requires a high concentration (at least the range of 1–7 µM) for dimerization.
source: UNC-104 requires a high concentration (at least the range of 1–7 µM) for dimerization (Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 mini-motors are enriched in phosphatidylinositol 4, 5-bisphosphate (PIP2) microdomains on artificial liposomes.
source: Furthermore, UNC-104 mini-motors, generated by deleting most of the stalk domains, have been shown to be enriched in phosphatidylinositol 4, 5-bisphosphate (PIP2) microdomains on artificial liposomes (Klopfenstein et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The UNC-104 mini-motor can efficiently transport PIP2-carrying vesicles in vitro.
source: As a result, the mini-motor can efficiently transport PIP2-carrying vesicles in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the prior statement about enrichment in PIP2 microdomains and is supported by citation.

claim: The non-processive UNC-104 monomer is accumulated to high concentrations and converted into an active dimer at PIP2 microdomains on the cargo membrane.
source: These results collectively suggested that the non-processive UNC-104 monomer is accumulated to high concentrations and converted into an active dimer at PIP2 microdomains on the cargo membrane (Klopfenstein et al., 2002; Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a model proposed in prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy analysis of UNC-104 and the X-ray structure of full-length KLP-6 have revealed the autoinhibited state of kinesin-3.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy analysis of UNC-104 and the X-ray structure of full-length KLP-6 have revealed the autoinhibited state of kinesin-3 (Al-Bassam et al., 2003; Ren et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Stalk domains, including CC1, FHA, and CC2 domains, bind to the motor domain and the neck coiled-coil domain and inhibit the microtubule-dependent motor activity of kinesin-3.
source: These structures suggest that stalk domains, including coiled-coil 1 (CC1), forkhead-associated (FHA), and coiled-coil 2 (CC2) domains, bind to the motor domain (MD) and the neck coiled-coil (NC) domain and inhibit the microtubule-dependent motor activity of kinesin-3 (Ren et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Point mutations that disrupt the autoinhibition of UNC-104 and KLP-6 have been identified based on genetic screening and crystal structure.
source: Based on the genetic screening and the crystal structure, point mutations that disrupt the autoinhibition of UNC-104 and KLP-6 have been identified.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies mentioned in the context.

claim: Prior studies have indirectly detected the activation of UNC-104 and KLP-6 by observing the localization of cargo vesicles, measuring ATPase activity or observing tip accumulation in neuronal cells.
source: These prior studies have indirectly detected the activation of UNC-104 and KLP-6 by observing the localization of cargo vesicles, measuring ATPase activity or observing tip accumulation in neuronal cells (Cong et al., 2021; Niwa et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The concentration of most cellular proteins is at the range of nanomolar.
source: Furthermore, confirming that UNC-104 and KLP-6 motors form dimers at physiological concentrations is necessary, since the concentration of most cellular proteins is at the range of nanomolar (Wühr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KLP-6FL was eluted from a single peak in size exclusion chromatography.
source: In a size exclusion chromatography (SEC), KLP-6FL was eluted from a single peak (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mass photometry confirmed that KLP-6FL was monomeric in solution.
source: Mass photometry confirmed that KLP-6FL was monomeric in solution (Figure 1C), as in the previous study (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data in Figure 1C and a citation to prior work.

claim: Purified KLP-6FL was an active microtubule-dependent motor in a microtubule gliding assay.
source: We found purified KLP-6FL was an active microtubule-dependent motor in a microtubule gliding assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The velocity of KLP-6FL movement in the gliding assay when attached via anti-GFP antibody (52.4±33.9 nm/s) was approximately 14-fold slower than that of KLP-6::GFP in cilia (0.72±0.18 µm/s).
source: In this condition, the velocity of the movement in the gliding assay (52.4±33.9 nm/s, mean ± standard deviation [SD], n=115 microtubules) was approximately 14-fold slower than that of KLP-6::GFP in cilia (0.72±0.18 µm/s) (Morsci and Barr, 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison with cited prior work.

claim: When KLP-6FL was attached on the glass surface directly, the velocity in the gliding assay increased to 154.9±20.3 µm/s.
source: Second, KLP-6FL was attached on the glass surface directly. This led to an increased velocity in the gliding assay (154.9±20.3 µm/s, mean ± SD, n=127 microtubules) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), implying that such attachment activates the motor in the gliding assay.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct attachment of KLP-6FL to the glass surface activates the motor in the gliding assay.
source: Second, KLP-6FL was attached on the glass surface directly. This led to an increased velocity in the gliding assay (154.9±20.3 µm/s, mean ± SD, n=127 microtubules) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), implying that such attachment activates the motor in the gliding assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased velocity upon direct attachment compared to antibody-mediated attachment.

claim: KLP-6FL bound to microtubules and exhibited one-dimensional diffusion, but rarely showed directional movement.
source: Our results showed that KLP-6FL bound to microtubules and exhibited one-dimensional diffusion, but rarely showed directional movement (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The tail domain of KLP-6, rather than the motor domain, binds to microtubules in the autoinhibited state.
source: While we observed KLP-6FL bound to microtubules and showed diffusion on microtubules (Figure 1D), the structure of KLP-6 shows that the stalk domains of KLP-6 cover its MD and prevent the MD from binding to microtubules (Wang et al., 2022). This raised a possibility that the tail domain of KLP-6, rather than the MD, bind to microtubules in the autoinhibited state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KLP-6FL binds microtubules despite structural evidence that the motor domain is blocked.

claim: KLP-6 (350–928), which lacks the motor domain, binds to microtubules.
source: We found that KLP-6 (350–928), which lacks the MD, and KLP-6 (580–928), which lacks the MD-NC-CC1-FHA domains, bound to microtubules (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KLP-6 (580–928), which lacks the MD-NC-CC1-FHA domains, binds to microtubules.
source: We found that KLP-6 (350–928), which lacks the MD, and KLP-6 (580–928), which lacks the MD-NC-CC1-FHA domains, bound to microtubules (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KLP-6 (1–390), which lacks the CC1-FHA-CC2 domains, was able to bind to microtubules.
source: However, KLP-6 (1–390), which lacks the CC1-FHA-CC2 domains, was able to bind to microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: None of the KLP-6 proteins showed processive movement on microtubules.
source: Note that none of the KLP-6 proteins showed processive movement on microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KLP-6 has a second microtubule binding domain in the tail domains.
source: These suggest that KLP-6 has a second microtubule binding domain in the tail domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tail domain constructs bind microtubules while motor domain constructs do not.

claim: KLP-6 (1–390) is an active microtubule-dependent motor in a microtubule gliding assay.
source: Although KLP-6 (1–390) did not show any processive runs on microtubules in the TIRF assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), we found KLP-6 (1–390) is an active microtubule-dependent motor in a microtubule gliding assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The velocity of microtubule gliding by KLP-6 (1–390) was 120.3±15.3 nm/s.
source: The motor was attached on the glass surface using the anti-GFP antibody and the velocity of microtubule gliding was 120.3±15.3 nm/s (mean ± SD, n=180 microtubules).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the gliding assay.

claim: Dimerization is required for kinesin-3 motors to achieve processive runs on microtubules.
source: For kinesin-3 motors, it has been proposed that dimerization is required to achieve processive runs on microtubules (Soppina et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KLP-6 (1–390)LZ moved on microtubules processively in the TIRF assay.
source: As a result, we found KLP-6 (1–390)LZ moved on microtubules processively in the TIRF assay (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The velocity of KLP-6 (1–390)LZ was 0.26±0.12 µm/s.
source: The velocity was 0.26±0.12 µm/s (mean ± SD, n=642 molecules).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TIRF assays.

claim: KLP-6 is an inactive monomer and requires dimerization to perform directional movement on microtubules.
source: These results suggest that KLP-6 is an inactive monomer and requires dimerization to perform directional movement on microtubules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that monomeric KLP-6 is non-processive while dimeric KLP-6(1-390)LZ is processive.

claim: UNC-104(1–653) is a monomeric and inactive protein.
source: In a previous study, UNC-104(1–653) was shown to be a monomeric and inactive protein, also known as U653 (Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KLP-6 (1–587) has a similar domain architecture to UNC-104(1-653).
source: KLP-6 (1–587) has a similar domain architecture to UNC-104(1-653) (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and was an inactive motor.
evidence: This is supported by domain comparison shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: KLP-6(D458A) mutation disrupts the intramolecular interaction between the FHA domain and motor domain.
source: Among mutations analyzed in their study, KLP-6(D458A), a mutation that disrupts the intramolecular interaction between the FHA domain and MD, has the strongest effect on the activation of KLP-6 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis cited from prior work and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: KLP-6(D458A) has the strongest effect on the activation of KLP-6 among mutations analyzed.
source: Among mutations analyzed in their study, KLP-6(D458A), a mutation that disrupts the intramolecular interaction between the FHA domain and MD, has the strongest effect on the activation of KLP-6 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) exhibited similar properties to wild-type KLP-6 (1–587) in the SEC analysis.
source: KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) exhibited similar properties to wild-type KLP-6 (1–587) in the SEC analysis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both KLP-6 (1–587) and KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) were predominantly monomeric in solution.
source: Subsequent mass photometry confirmed that both KLP-6 (1–587) and KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) were predominantly monomeric in solution (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: KLP-6 (1–587) exhibited comparable activity to KLP-6 (1–390) in the microtubule gliding assay.
source: Under the condition of the microtubule gliding assay with the anti-GFP antibody, KLP-6 (1–587) (116.7±17.9 nm/s, mean ± SD, n=107 microtubules) as well as KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) (114.3±18.9 nm/s, mean ± SD, n=103 microtubules) exhibited comparable activity to KLP-6 (1–390) (120.3±15.3 nm/s, mean ± SD, n=180 microtubules) even without attaching the motor to the surface directly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A), but not wild-type KLP-6 (1–587), frequently bound to microtubules in the TIRF assay.
source: Despite these similar properties between KLP-6 (1–587) and KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) in the gliding assay, KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A), but not wild-type KLP-6 (1–587), frequently bound to microtubules in the TIRF assay (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) only exhibited one-dimensional diffusion and did not show any processive runs on microtubules.
source: However, KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) only exhibited one-dimensional diffusion and did not show any processive runs on microtubules (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The autoinhibition of KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) is relieved but KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) still cannot form processive dimers.
source: Considering that dimeric KLP-6 (1–390)LZ, but not monomeric KLP-6 (1–390), are processive, these observations indicate that the autoinhibition of KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) is relieved but that KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) still cannot form processive dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of KLP-6 (1–587)(D458A) with KLP-6 (1–390)LZ.

claim: UNC-104(E412K) mutation disrupts the autoinhibition of UNC-104.
source: Our previous work has identified mutations in the CC1 domain of UNC-104, such as UNC-104(E412K), that activate axonal transport of synaptic vesicle precursors (Niwa et al., 2016). Autoinhibited KLP-6 and KIF13B structures suggest that the E412K mutation in the UNC-104 disrupts the autoinhibition of UNC-104 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) similarly to the KLP-6(D458A) mutation (Ren et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by prior genetic studies and structural analysis.

claim: UNC-104(1–653) exhibited two peaks in the SEC analysis, corresponding to the size of dimers and monomers.
source: UNC-104(1–653) exhibited two peaks in the SEC analysis (Figure 5B), corresponding to the size of dimers and monomers, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: UNC-104(1–653) predominantly eluted in the monomer peak.
source: UNC-104(1–653) predominantly eluted in the monomer peak (Figure 5B, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The monomeric fraction of UNC-104(1–653) re-equilibrated into two peaks after incubation.
source: This monomer peak fraction was subjected to a re-run in the SEC analysis. After incubating for sufficient time, we observed that the monomeric fraction re-equilibrated into two peaks, resembling the results from the initial SEC analysis of UNC-104(1–653) (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) eluted in a single peak whose expected molecular weight was that of a dimer.
source: Unlike KLP-6 (1–587), UNC-104(1–653) exhibited a clear peak shift in the SEC analysis by introducing a mutation to relieve the autoinhibition (Figure 5B). UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) eluted in a single peak whose expected molecular weight was that of a dimer.
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Wild-type UNC-104(1–653) was mostly monomeric with less than 5% of dimers detected by mass photometry.
source: Mass photometry revealed that wild-type UNC-104(1–653) was mostly monomeric (Figure 5C, blue), with less than 5% of dimers detected.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) was a mixture of monomers and dimers with the ratio almost 1:1.
source: In contrast, UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) was a mixture of monomers and dimers (Figure 5C, orange), with the ratio of monomers and dimers almost 1:1.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The difference between SEC and mass photometry results can be attributed to the concentration disparity between the two techniques.
source: It is likely that the difference between SEC and mass photometry can be attributed to the concentration disparity between the two techniques; SEC operates in the micromolar range, while mass photometry operates in the nanomolar range, as further discussed later.
evidence: This is inferred from the known concentration ranges of the two techniques.

claim: Wild-type UNC-104(1–653) exhibited a trace number of processive runs on microtubules purified from brain tissues but not on Chlamydomonas axonemes.
source: The prior study showed that UNC-104(1–653) does not show any processive runs on Chlamydomonas axonemes, which were widely used in the single molecule assays (Tomishige et al., 2002). However, we found wild-type UNC-104(1–653) exhibited a trace number of processive runs on microtubules purified from brain tissues but not on Chlamydomonas axonemes (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) very frequently exhibited processive movement on purified microtubules.
source: Furthermore, UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) very frequently exhibited processive movement on purified microtubules (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: The velocity of moving particles did not differ significantly between UNC-104(1–653) and UNC-104(1–653)(E412K).
source: Although the velocity of moving particles did not differ significantly (Figure 5F), the run length of UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) was much longer than that of wild-type UNC-104(1–653) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The run length of UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) was much longer than that of wild-type UNC-104(1–653).
source: Although the velocity of moving particles did not differ significantly (Figure 5F), the run length of UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) was much longer than that of wild-type UNC-104(1–653) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The equilibrium between monomers and dimers is shifted toward the dimer form when the autoinhibition of UNC-104 is released.
source: These results suggest that the equilibrium between monomers and dimers is shifted toward the dimer form when the autoinhibition of UNC-104 is released.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC and mass photometry data showing increased dimer formation in E412K mutant.

claim: KLP-6(E409K) did not convert to dimers.
source: Finally, we confirmed that the difference between UNC-104 and KLP-6 is not due to the effect of different mutations because KLP-6(E409K) did not convert to dimers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CC2 domain of KLP-6 is much shorter than UNC-104.
source: The sequences of KLP-6 (1–587) and UNC-104(1–653) are very similar, except that the CC2 domain of KLP-6 is much shorter than UNC-104 as depicted in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The probability of coiled-coil formation for the CC2 domain of KLP-6 is very low according to Marcoil algorithm.
source: Although the X-ray structure of monomeric KLP-6 has suggested a short α-helix domain is the CC2 domain of KLP-6 (Wang et al., 2022), the probability of coiled-coil formation expected from the Marcoil algorism is very low (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by coiled-coil prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The CC2 domain of UNC-104 is expected to be a conventional coiled coil with a high probability.
source: On the other hand, the CC2 domain of UNC-104 is expected to be a conventional coiled coil with a high probability (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by coiled-coil prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UNC-104CC2, but not KLP-6CC2, is capable to induce dimerization.
source: While the peak of KLP-6CC2-mScarlet was indistinguishable from mScarlet alone, UNC-104CC2-mScarlet exhibited a clear peak shift (Figure 6C). The analysis indicates that UNC-104CC2, but not KLP-6CC2, is capable to induce dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both UNC-104(1–594) and UNC-104(1–594)(E412K) showed almost identical profiles in SEC analysis.
source: In the SEC analysis, both UNC-104(1–594) and UNC-104(1–594)(E412K) showed almost identical profiles (Figure 7B), which totally differed from the results that UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) shifted toward higher molecular weights compared to UNC-104(1–653) which presents two elution peaks (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both UNC-104(1–594) and UNC-104(1–594)(E412K) were predominantly monomeric in solution.
source: Mass photometry showed that both UNC-104(1–594) and UNC-104(1–594) (E412K) were predominantly monomeric in solution (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: UNC-104(1–594) rarely showed processive runs on microtubules at the nanomolar range.
source: TIRF microscopy analysis demonstrated that, UNC-104(1–594) rarely showed processive runs on microtubules at the nanomolar range.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data described in the text.

claim: The run length and landing rate of UNC-104(1–594)(E412K) were much lower than those of UNC-104(1–653)(E412K).
source: While UNC-104(1–594) (E412K) displayed some processive runs on microtubules, the run length and landing rate were much lower than those of UNC-104(1–653)(E412K) (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-G.

claim: The CC2 domain is required for the stable dimer formation, activation, and processive runs of UNC-104.
source: These results suggest that the CC2 domain is required for the stable dimer formation, activation, and processive runs of UNC-104.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of UNC-104(1-594) and UNC-104(1-653) constructs.

claim: UNC-104(L640F) mutation reduces the axonal transport of synaptic materials in C. elegans.
source: To confirm the importance of CC2-dependent dimerization in the axonal transport, we proceeded to biochemically analyze a mutation within the CC2 domain of UNC-104. The mutation, UNC-104(L640F), reduces the axonal transport of synaptic materials in C. elegans (Cong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 (1–653) (E412K, L640F) predominantly eluted in the monomer peak.
source: SEC analysis showed that UNC-104 (1–653) (E412K, L640F) predominantly eluted in the monomer peak, even though E412K mitigated autoinhibition and promoted dimerization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The in vitro result of UNC-104 (1–653) (E412K, L640F) is consistent with abnormal accumulation of synaptic vesicles in unc-104(L640F) worms.
source: This in vitro result is consistent with abnormal accumulation of synaptic vesicles in unc-104(L640F) worms.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: UNC-104(1–653) is able to form active dimers at micromolar concentrations.
source: Our SEC analysis showed that UNC-104(1–653) was a mixture of dimers and monomers, with monomers predominating (Figure 5B). A prior study has observed similar phenomena. UNC-104(1–653) is able to form active dimers at micromolar concentrations (Tomishige et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and SEC data.

claim: UNC-104 exists in an equilibrium between monomers and dimers.
source: These results suggest that (1) UNC-104 exists in an equilibrium between monomers and dimers and (2) the release of the autoinhibition, such as by UNC-104(E412K) mutation, shifts the state of the equilibrium toward the formation of dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC and mass photometry data showing concentration-dependent oligomeric states.

claim: The release of the autoinhibition shifts the state of the equilibrium toward the formation of dimers in UNC-104.
source: These results suggest that (1) UNC-104 exists in an equilibrium between monomers and dimers and (2) the release of the autoinhibition, such as by UNC-104(E412K) mutation, shifts the state of the equilibrium toward the formation of dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type and E412K mutant UNC-104.

claim: The CC2 domain has been demonstrated to be crucial for the autoinhibition of KIF1A and UNC-104.
source: The CC2 domain has been demonstrated to be crucial for the autoinhibition of KIF1A and UNC-104 (Hammond et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The E612K mutation in the CC2 domain of UNC-104 disrupts its autoinhibition.
source: We have previously shown that the E612K mutation in the CC2 domain of UNC-104 disrupt its autoinhibition (Niwa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Crystal structure analysis revealed that the short CC2 domain of KLP-6 is involved in autoinhibition.
source: Moreover, crystal structure analysis revealed that the short CC2 domain of KLP-6 is also involved in autoinhibition.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis, likely from cited prior work.

claim: CC2 domain is required for cargo binding in kinesin-3.
source: Moreover, crystal structure analysis revealed that the short CC2 domain of KLP-6 is also involved in autoinhibition. In addition to the role in the autoinhibition, CC2 domain is required for the cargo binding (Hummel and Hoogenraad, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CC2 is required for the full activation and processivity of kinesin-3.
source: We suggest here that, in addition to these functions, CC2 is required for the full activation and processivity of kinesin-3.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing constructs with and without CC2.

claim: A deletion mutant of KIF13B composed of MD, NC, and CC1 can form a dimer when the autoinhibition is unlocked by mutations, but the major population remains monomeric.
source: A prior work has shown that a deletion mutant of KIF13B composed of MD, NC, and CC1 can form a dimer when the autoinhibition is unlocked by mutations, but the major population remains monomeric in the ultracentrifugation analysis (Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The monomer-to-dimer conversion was observed upon release of the autoinhibition in the case of the full length of KIF13B which has the CC2 domain.
source: Indeed, the monomer-to-dimer conversion was observed upon release of the autoinhibition in the case of the full length of KIF13B which has the CC2 domain (Fan and McKenney, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The CC2 domain is conserved in most of the kinesin-3 family proteins including KIF1Bα, KIF1C, KIF13A, KIF16A, and KIF16B.
source: The CC2 domain is conserved in most of the kinesin-3 family proteins including KIF1Bα, KIF1C, KIF13A, KIF16A, and KIF16B (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The CC2 domain is fundamental to the stable dimer formation in kinesin-3.
source: Taken together, we suggest that the CC2 domain is fundamental to the stable dimer formation in kinesin-3.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with other kinesin-3 family members.

claim: The CC2 domain is required for UNC-104 to move long distances on microtubules.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that the CC2 domain is required for UNC-104 to move long distances on microtubules (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-G.

claim: Without the CC2 domain, UNC-104 shows only very short runs even if they are activated for microtubule binding.
source: Without the CC2 domain, UNC-104 shows only very short runs even if they are activated for microtubule binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing UNC-104(1-594) and UNC-104(1-653).

claim: The CC2 domain is essential for long-distance transport, such as axonal transport.
source: Therefore, the CC2 domain would be essential for long-distance transport, such as axonal transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CC2 is required for long processive runs.

claim: The CC2 mutation, unc-104(L640F), reduces the amount of axonal transport in vivo.
source: Consistent with this idea, the CC2 mutation, unc-104(L640F), which inhibits efficient dimerization of UNC-104 in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), reduces the amount of axonal transport in vivo (Cong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior research.

claim: The extensive post-translational modifications and the presence of microtubule binding proteins on Chlamydomonas axonemes potentially inhibits the motility of kinesins.
source: Neither Tomishige et al. nor we were able to observe any processive runs of wild-type UNC-104(1-653) on Chlamydomonas axonemes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Tomishige et al., 2002). Moreover, the motility of KIF1A(1-393)LZ was less frequent on Chlamydomonas axonemes compared with microtubules purified from brain tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). These observation might be attributed to the extensive post-translational modifications and the presence of microtubule binding proteins on Chlamydomonas axonemes, which potentially inhibits the motility of kinesins.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed differences in motility between axonemes and purified microtubules.

claim: Processive movements of UNC-104 can be observed even at nanomolar concentrations when employing purified porcine microtubules as the tracks.
source: In contrast, we show that processive movements of UNC-104 can be observed even at nanomolar concentrations when employing purified porcine microtubules as the tracks.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TIRF assays.

claim: The release of autoinhibition is sufficient for monomeric UNC-104 to dimerize and move processively on microtubules at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: Moreover, our study provides compelling evidence that the release of autoinhibition is sufficient for monomeric UNC-104 to dimerize and move processively on microtubules at low nanomolar concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mass photometry and TIRF assays.

claim: KIF1A needs to form a homodimer to bind to cargo vesicles.
source: A recent study has shown that KIF1A, a mammalian ortholog of UNC-104, needs to form a homodimer to bind to cargo vesicles, indicating that KIF1A dimerizes before interacting with cargo vesicles, rather than on cargo vesicles (Hummel and Hoogenraad, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KIF1A dimerizes before interacting with cargo vesicles, rather than on cargo vesicles.
source: A recent study has shown that KIF1A, a mammalian ortholog of UNC-104, needs to form a homodimer to bind to cargo vesicles, indicating that KIF1A dimerizes before interacting with cargo vesicles, rather than on cargo vesicles (Hummel and Hoogenraad, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: UNC-104 forms dimers in cytosol upon release of autoinhibition, rather than on cargo vesicles, as a prerequisite for motor activation and cargo binding.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that UNC-104 forms dimers in cytosol upon release of autoinhibition, rather than on cargo vesicles, as a prerequisite for motor activation and cargo binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and comparison with KIF1A.

claim: The amount of synaptic vesicles transported by UNC-104 is increased by the UNC-104(E412K) mutation.
source: Indeed, the amount of synaptic vesicles transported by UNC-104 is increased by the UNC-104(E412K) mutation (Niwa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PIP2 microdomains may play a role in stabilizing UNC-104 dimers to ensure long-distance axonal transport.
source: It is possible that PIP2 microdomains may play a role in stabilizing UNC-104 dimers to ensure long-distance axonal transport because UNC-104 dimers are more stable at higher concentrations even when the autoinhibition is unlocked (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is speculated based on the concentration-dependent stability of dimers.

claim: LOV-1 and PKD-2, which form the mechanoreceptor complex transported by KLP-6, stand as potential candidates for an additional regulatory role in KLP-6 dimerization.
source: LOV-1 and PKD-2, which form the mechanoreceptor complex transported by KLP-6, stand as potential candidates for an additional regulatory role in KLP-6 dimerization.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that KLP-6 does not dimerize on its own.

claim: KLP-6 can be activated in Neuro 2a cells when autoinhibition is unlocked.
source: However, KLP-6 can be activated in Neuro 2a cells when autoinhibition is unlocked (Wang et al., 2022), implying that other unidentified factors, including post-translational modifications and binding proteins, may be required for KLP-6 dimerization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Other unidentified factors, including post-translational modifications and binding proteins, may be required for KLP-6 dimerization.
source: However, KLP-6 can be activated in Neuro 2a cells when autoinhibition is unlocked (Wang et al., 2022), implying that other unidentified factors, including post-translational modifications and binding proteins, may be required for KLP-6 dimerization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is speculated based on the difference between in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: Mutations disrupting autoinhibition of KLP-6, such as D458A mutation, may enhance the intraflagellar transport of LOV-1 and PKD-2 complex in C. elegans.
source: Our findings imply that mutations disrupting autoinhibition of KLP-6, such as D458A mutation, enhance the intraflagellar transport of LOV-1 and PKD-2 complex in C. elegans.
evidence: This is speculated based on the in vitro findings and prior in vivo observations.
